en.correct: a musical texture consisting of two or more independent melodic lines sounding together
distractors: a single melodic line performed without any accompaniment
the use of only chords built in stacked thirds

example.text: The motet's polyphony wove four independent vocal lines into a single texture.

en.correct: a texture in which one main melody is supported by subordinate chordal accompaniment
distractors: a texture built from several equally important independent melodies
music performed entirely in unison by all voices

example.text: Chorale settings are typically homophony, with the melody carried by the top voice over block chords.

en.correct: a texture in which multiple performers simultaneously vary the same basic melody
distractors: a texture of two unrelated melodies played in different keys
a single melodic line doubled exactly at the octave

example.text: In the folk ensemble, heterophony emerged as each fiddler ornamented the shared tune slightly differently.

en.correct: the technique of combining two or more independent melodic lines according to rules governing their relationship
distractors: the practice of harmonizing a melody with a single chord per bar
the study of instrumental tone color

example.text: Bach's counterpoint interlaces four voices so each retains its own melodic logic.

en.correct: relating to or written in the style of counterpoint, with independent interweaving melodic lines
distractors: relating to music built entirely from block chords
relating to strictly improvised, unnotated music

example.text: The fugue's contrapuntal texture demands that each entering voice remain melodically independent.

en.correct: a combination of tones that sounds tense or unstable and seeks resolution
distractors: a chord built exclusively from stacked thirds
the steady pulse underlying a piece of music

example.text: The dissonance of the suspended fourth resolved smoothly down to the third.

en.correct: a combination of tones that sounds stable and does not require resolution
distractors: a rapid alternation between two adjacent pitches
the deliberate blurring of the beat through off-accents

example.text: The phrase ended on a consonance, giving the listener a clear sense of arrival.

en.correct: a harmonic or melodic formula that marks the end of a phrase, section, or piece
distractors: a repeating rhythmic pattern maintained under a changing melody
the overall range of pitches a voice or instrument can produce

example.text: The final cadence resolved firmly onto the tonic chord.

en.correct: the process of moving from one key to another within a piece of music
distractors: the gradual increase in loudness over a phrase
the doubling of a melodic line at the octave

example.text: The bridge achieves a modulation from C major to the relative minor.

en.correct: to shift a passage of music from one key to another
distractors: to double a melodic line in parallel octaves
to slow the tempo gradually toward the end of a phrase

example.text: The composer modulates to the dominant just before the second theme.

en.correct: a rhythmic effect created by accenting beats or parts of beats that are normally weak
distractors: the simultaneous sounding of two different keys
the exact repetition of a melodic phrase a step higher

example.text: The syncopation in the bass line pushes accents onto the off-beats.

en.correct: to shift rhythmic accents onto normally unaccented beats or offbeats
distractors: to combine two independent melodic lines contrapuntally
to raise a passage by a fixed interval into a new key

example.text: The arranger syncopated the melody to give it a jazzier feel.

en.correct: the range of pitches in which a particular voice or instrumental part lies most comfortably and is used most often
distractors: the total possible pitch range of an instrument from lowest to highest note
a short cadenza-like passage inserted before a final cadence

example.text: The aria's high tessitura suits a lyric soprano rather than a mezzo.

en.correct: the distinctive tone color or quality of a sound that distinguishes one instrument or voice from another
distractors: the loudness of a sound measured over time
the precise duration of a single note

example.text: The oboe's reedy timbre cuts through the orchestral texture.

en.correct: a short musical pattern that is repeated persistently, usually in the same voice or register
distractors: a sudden unexpected change of key
a passage played freely without strict tempo

example.text: A driving bass ostinato underpins the entire movement.

en.correct: a recurring musical theme associated with a particular character, idea, or situation, especially in opera or film
distractors: a short cadential formula used to end a phrase
a scale built from alternating whole and half steps

example.text: Wagner assigns a distinct leitmotif to each major character in the cycle.

en.correct: the simultaneous use of two or more conflicting rhythmic patterns or meters
distractors: a single rhythm that gradually slows down and speeds up
the practice of doubling a rhythm exactly an octave apart

example.text: The drummer layered a polyrhythm of three against two across the ensemble.

en.correct: a rhythmic device in which two bars of triple meter are reinterpreted as three bars of duple meter, or the reverse
distractors: a scale that alternates major and minor thirds
a cadence that avoids resolving to the expected tonic

example.text: Brahms uses a hemiola near the cadence to blur the sense of triple meter.

en.correct: the compositional technique of restating a melodic idea in longer note values than its original form
distractors: the technique of restating a melodic idea backward from end to beginning
the process of adding extra voices to a previously solo texture

example.text: The fugue's final entry presents the subject in augmentation, doubling every note's duration.

en.correct: the compositional technique of restating a melodic idea in shorter note values than its original form
distractors: the technique of inverting a melody so it moves in the opposite direction
the gradual reduction of the number of instruments playing

example.text: The composer answers the theme with a diminution, compressing it into half the original time.

en.correct: a rearrangement of a chord, interval, or melody, such as reordering chord tones or flipping a melodic line's direction
distractors: the exact repetition of a phrase at a different pitch level
the simultaneous combination of two keys

example.text: The subject returns in inversion, with every ascending interval now descending.

en.correct: to rearrange a musical element, such as flipping a melody's direction or reordering a chord's notes
distractors: to slow a rhythmic pattern to twice its original duration
to combine two unrelated themes into a single passage

example.text: The composer inverts the opening motif so its rising line now falls.

en.correct: a version of a melody or theme played with its original note order reversed, from last note to first
distractors: a melody played with its rhythm doubled in speed
a chord progression that avoids returning to the tonic

example.text: The final variation presents the theme in retrograde, unfolding backward from its last note.

en.correct: the immediate repetition of a melodic or harmonic pattern at a new pitch level
distractors: a chord built by stacking notes a fourth apart instead of a third
the point where a piece changes from one meter to another

example.text: The violin line rises through a sequence, repeating the same figure a step higher each time.

en.correct: a sustained or repeated note, usually in the bass, held while the harmonies above it change
distractors: a brief silent gap inserted between two phrases
a note approached and left by step that is not part of the underlying chord

example.text: The organ sustains a pedal point on the dominant beneath the shifting upper harmonies.

en.correct: a note held over from one chord into the next, creating a dissonance that then resolves downward by step
distractors: a chord that omits its third to sound ambiguous
a sudden unprepared change of dynamic level

example.text: The 4-3 suspension delays the resolution to the tonic chord by one beat.

en.correct: a suspension-like dissonance that is held over and then resolves upward by step instead of downward
distractors: a general slowing of tempo across an entire movement
a chord progression that repeats itself exactly a fourth higher

example.text: The soprano's retardation resolves upward into the final tonic chord, unlike a typical suspension.

en.correct: an ornamental note approached by a leap that falls on a strong beat and resolves by step into the following chord tone
distractors: a note that connects two chord tones by moving stepwise on a weak beat
a chord formed entirely of intervals of a fourth

example.text: The soprano's appoggiatura leans dissonantly into the downbeat before settling onto the chord tone.

en.correct: a note that sounds before its chord arrives, briefly anticipating a tone of the coming harmony
distractors: a note held over from the previous chord that resolves downward by step
a rest inserted to delay the arrival of a cadence

example.text: The melody's anticipation sounds the new tonic note just before the harmony actually changes.

en.correct: a non-chord tone that fills the stepwise space between two chord tones
distractors: a note approached by leap that resolves by step on a strong beat
a tone sustained across several changing harmonies

example.text: A passing tone connects the third and fifth of the chord by stepwise motion.

en.correct: a non-chord tone that steps away from a chord tone and then returns to the same chord tone
distractors: a note that is repeated identically in every voice of a chord
a tone that leaps away from a chord tone and resolves to a different chord tone

example.text: The upper neighbor tone decorates the melody before returning to the original pitch.

en.correct: a non-chord tone that is left by step and resolves by leap in the opposite direction
distractors: a non-chord tone approached by leap and left by step
a chord tone that is deliberately omitted from the texture

example.text: The escape tone steps away from the chord tone, then leaps back down to the next harmony.

en.correct: a melodic figure in which a note is left by a skip to a non-chord tone that then resolves stepwise into the harmony
distractors: a chord that substitutes a raised fourth for the fifth
a rhythmic pattern created by tying notes across the barline

example.text: The cambiata in the alto line briefly steps outside the harmony before resolving.

en.correct: the first scale degree of a key, serving as its central tone of rest and resolution
distractors: the fifth scale degree, which typically precedes a cadence
the note a half step below the tonic that pulls toward it

example.text: The piece firmly establishes C as its tonic in the opening bars.

en.correct: the fifth scale degree of a key, whose chord characteristically drives toward resolution on the tonic
distractors: the first scale degree, functioning as the tonal center of a key
the sixth scale degree, which often substitutes for the tonic in a deceptive cadence

example.text: The dominant chord builds tension that resolves onto the tonic at the cadence.

en.correct: the fourth scale degree of a key, whose chord often precedes the dominant in a progression
distractors: the second scale degree, typically used to introduce the dominant
the seventh scale degree, which leads strongly upward to the tonic

example.text: The plagal cadence moves from the subdominant directly to the tonic.

en.correct: the third scale degree of a key, situated midway between the tonic and dominant
distractors: the sixth scale degree, lying midway between the subdominant and tonic an octave above
the note a half step below the tonic

example.text: The chord built on the mediant often substitutes for the tonic in a deceptive progression.

en.correct: the sixth scale degree of a key, whose chord commonly receives the deceptive cadence
distractors: the third scale degree, lying between the tonic and dominant
the leading tone, a half step below the tonic

example.text: In the deceptive cadence, the dominant resolves to the submediant instead of the tonic.

en.correct: the seventh scale degree of a major or harmonic minor key, a half step below the tonic, with a strong pull toward it
distractors: the fifth scale degree, which forms the dominant chord
a non-chord tone that connects two chord tones stepwise

example.text: The leading tone resolves upward by half step into the tonic at the cadence.

en.correct: the use of notes outside a key's diatonic scale, typically moving by half step
distractors: the exclusive use of a key's own scale tones without alteration
the practice of doubling a melody at the interval of an octave

example.text: The late Romantic harmony is saturated with chromaticism that obscures the underlying key.

en.correct: describing two different note names that represent the same pitch, such as F sharp and G flat
distractors: describing a chord built from stacked fourths rather than thirds
describing a melody that is played simultaneously in two different keys

example.text: The composer respells the chord enharmonically to prepare an unexpected modulation.

en.correct: using only the notes belonging to a given major or minor scale, without chromatic alteration
distractors: using notes from outside the prevailing key, typically moving by half step
built from intervals of a fourth stacked on top of one another

example.text: The opening theme stays strictly diatonic within the key of G major.

en.correct: lacking a central key or tonal center, so no single pitch functions as a point of resolution
distractors: written using only the seven notes of a major scale
centered firmly on a single tonic throughout

example.text: Schoenberg's early free atonal pieces abandon traditional key relationships entirely.

en.correct: the simultaneous use of two or more different keys in different musical layers
distractors: the rapid alternation between two different meters
the practice of writing a melody using only a twelve-tone row

example.text: Stravinsky layers polytonality by combining a C major and F-sharp major triad simultaneously.

en.correct: the quality of a piece derived from its use of a mode, such as Dorian or Mixolydian, rather than major or minor tonality
distractors: the specific tempo marking assigned at the start of a piece
the total number of independent voices in a texture

example.text: The folk tune's modality gives it a distinctly Dorian flavor rather than a minor-key sound.

en.correct: a cadence that moves from the subdominant chord to the tonic chord, often called the amen cadence
distractors: a cadence that moves from the dominant chord to the tonic chord
a cadence that ends on a chord other than the tonic

example.text: The hymn closes with a plagal cadence beneath the final amen.

en.correct: a cadence that moves from the dominant chord to the tonic chord, providing a strong sense of closure
distractors: a cadence that moves from the subdominant chord to the tonic chord
a cadence that ends on the dominant chord, leaving the phrase open

example.text: The movement concludes with a perfect authentic cadence in the home key.

en.correct: a cadence in which the dominant chord resolves to a chord other than the tonic, usually the submediant, frustrating the expected resolution
distractors: a cadence that ends squarely and predictably on the tonic chord
a cadence formed entirely of parallel perfect fifths

example.text: Just before the final cadence, the composer inserts a deceptive cadence to prolong the phrase.

en.correct: a cadence that ends on the dominant chord, creating a sense of pause rather than final closure
distractors: a cadence that ends firmly on the tonic chord
a cadence in which the dominant resolves to the submediant

example.text: The first phrase ends with a half cadence, leaving the harmony unresolved.

en.correct: a cadence in minor keys where the subdominant in first inversion moves to the dominant, characteristic of Baroque slow movements
distractors: a cadence that ends on the tonic chord in root position
a cadence built entirely from a whole-tone scale

example.text: The slow movement closes with a Phrygian cadence leading into the following Allegro.

en.correct: the raising of the third of a final tonic chord in a minor-key piece so that it ends on a major chord
distractors: a chord that substitutes a lowered second scale degree for the tonic
an ornament that decorates a cadence with a rapid alternation of two pitches

example.text: The minor-key fugue ends unexpectedly with a Picardy third, brightening the final chord.

en.correct: the interval spanning three whole tones, such as an augmented fourth or diminished fifth, historically considered unstable
distractors: the interval of a perfect fifth between two chord tones
a chord built from four stacked minor thirds

example.text: The dominant seventh chord's tritone drives its strong pull toward resolution.

en.correct: the manner in which individual musical lines move from chord to chord, typically by the smallest practical intervals
distractors: the assignment of instruments to specific melodic lines in an orchestral score
the process of transposing an entire piece into a new key

example.text: Smooth voice leading keeps each inner part moving by step wherever possible.

en.correct: a system of numerals placed below a bass line indicating the chords and intervals to be played above it
distractors: a bass line doubled an octave lower by a second instrument
a melodic ornament consisting of a rapid alternation between two notes

example.text: The keyboardist realizes the figured bass, improvising chords from the numerals beneath the bass notes.

en.correct: a continuous bass line, typically realized by keyboard and a bass instrument, that underpins Baroque ensemble music
distractors: a solo cadenza performed without accompaniment near a movement's end
a melodic line doubled in parallel thirds throughout a piece

example.text: The harpsichord and cello together provide the basso continuo beneath the singers.

en.correct: a preexisting melody, often drawn from chant, used as the structural foundation for a new polyphonic composition
distractors: a melody composed entirely of chromatic passing tones
the highest voice in a four-part vocal texture

example.text: The Renaissance mass sets a chant cantus firmus in long notes in the tenor voice.

en.correct: a contrapuntal composition in which a subject is introduced by one voice and then imitated in turn by the others
distractors: a piece built from a single repeated ostinato bass with no imitation
a composition consisting of a theme followed by successive variations

example.text: The fugue's subject enters first in the alto, then is answered in the soprano a fifth higher.

en.correct: a passage, especially in a fugue, where successive entries of the subject overlap closely before the previous entry finishes
distractors: a slow, freely improvised passage inserted before a final cadence
a section where all voices pause simultaneously

example.text: The fugue builds intensity through a stretto in which the subject enters in quick succession.

en.correct: a secondary melodic idea in a fugue that regularly accompanies the subject in counterpoint
distractors: the opening statement of the main theme in a fugue's first voice
a chord progression that returns the music to the home key

example.text: The countersubject weaves against the subject each time it reappears in a new voice.

en.correct: a contrapuntal composition in which one voice strictly imitates another at a fixed time interval
distractors: a piece consisting of a single melody with no imitation at all
a set of variations on a repeated bass pattern

example.text: The round is a simple canon in which each voice enters singing the identical melody in turn.

en.correct: a musical form in which a recurring main theme alternates with contrasting episodes
distractors: a form consisting of a single theme repeated with continuous rhythmic variation only
a form built from an exposition, development, and recapitulation of two contrasting themes

example.text: The finale is a lively rondo whose refrain returns after each contrasting episode.

en.correct: the section of sonata form that restates the exposition's themes, typically all in the home key
distractors: the opening section of sonata form that first presents the primary and secondary themes
the central section of sonata form where thematic material is fragmented and explored

example.text: The recapitulation brings back the second theme, now transposed into the tonic key.

en.correct: a concluding passage appended to a movement or piece, extending the final cadential material
distractors: the opening thematic statement of a sonata-form movement
a passage in which two independent themes are combined simultaneously

example.text: The symphony ends with an extended coda that reaffirms the tonic key.

en.correct: a lively, often rhythmically playful movement in triple meter, frequently used in place of a minuet
distractors: a slow, lyrical movement typically placed second in a multi-movement work
a movement built entirely on variations of a single ground bass

example.text: Beethoven's scherzo replaces the courtly minuet with a fast, energetic triple-meter movement.

en.correct: describing a vocal work in which new music is written for each stanza of text rather than repeating the same music
distractors: describing a piece built from a single repeated strophe of music for every stanza
describing a piece composed collaboratively by more than one composer

example.text: Schubert's setting is through-composed, with fresh music tracking the poem's shifting imagery.

en.correct: describing a vocal work in which the same music is repeated for each stanza of text
distractors: describing a vocal work in which entirely new music accompanies each stanza of text
describing a piece with no fixed meter or steady pulse

example.text: The folk song is strophic, using identical music for all five verses.

en.correct: a medieval and early Renaissance compositional technique that repeats a fixed rhythmic pattern independently of the accompanying melodic pattern
distractors: a technique in which a melody is repeated at a progressively faster tempo
the simultaneous performance of two entirely different meters

example.text: The motet's tenor voice organizes its isorhythm around a repeating rhythmic pattern beneath varying pitches.

en.correct: the repeating rhythmic pattern used in an isorhythmic composition, independent of its melodic pattern
distractors: the repeating pitch pattern used in an isorhythmic composition, independent of its rhythm
a short cadenza inserted between two structural sections

example.text: The tenor's talea repeats every twelve measures while the melodic pattern spans a longer cycle.

en.correct: a compositional method that organizes musical elements, especially pitch, according to a fixed ordered series
distractors: a style of composition centered on tonal harmony and functional chord progressions
the practice of improvising freely without any predetermined structure

example.text: Webern's serialism applies a strict twelve-tone ordering to every pitch in the piece.

en.correct: a twelve-tone compositional method in which all twelve chromatic pitches are treated as equally important, organized through a fixed row
distractors: a scale system using only eight alternating whole and half steps
a texture built from twelve simultaneous independent melodic lines

example.text: Schoenberg pioneered dodecaphony as a systematic alternative to traditional tonal harmony.

en.correct: a fixed ordering of the twelve chromatic pitches used as the basis for a twelve-tone composition
distractors: a scale consisting of only whole-tone intervals
a chord built by stacking all twelve pitches simultaneously

example.text: The composer derives the entire piece's melodic and harmonic material from a single tone row.

en.correct: involving an element of chance or indeterminacy left to the performer's choice in a composition
distractors: strictly notated so that every performance sounds identical
based entirely on a preexisting twelve-tone row

example.text: In the aleatoric passage, performers choose the order of the notated fragments themselves.

en.correct: a compositional approach that derives musical material from the analysis of a sound's acoustic overtone spectrum
distractors: a compositional approach based strictly on a fixed twelve-tone row
a style built entirely on repeating diatonic patterns with gradual phase shifts

example.text: Grisey's spectralism shapes the orchestration around the overtone series of a single low note.

en.correct: the use of intervals smaller than the conventional semitone of Western equal temperament
distractors: the use of only the twelve equal semitones of standard tuning
the practice of doubling every interval at the octave

example.text: The composer's microtonality divides the octave into quarter tones rather than semitones.

en.correct: a tuning system based on pure whole-number frequency ratios between pitches, rather than equal divisions of the octave
distractors: a tuning system that divides the octave into twelve equal semitones
a system in which every interval is deliberately tuned slightly out of tune for effect

example.text: The vocal ensemble tunes its chords in just intonation to achieve especially pure harmonies.

en.correct: a tuning system that divides the octave into twelve equal semitones, allowing music to modulate freely between keys
distractors: a tuning system based on pure whole-number frequency ratios between pitches
a system in which only diatonic intervals are permitted

example.text: Modern pianos are tuned in equal temperament so every key sounds equally in tune.

en.correct: the shifting of a piece or passage of music from one pitch level or key to another while preserving its intervallic relationships
distractors: the reordering of a melody's notes from last to first
the doubling of a melodic line at the interval of a fourth

example.text: The clarinet part requires transposition down a whole step from the written pitch.

en.correct: to rewrite or perform a piece of music at a different pitch level while keeping its intervals intact
distractors: to reverse the order of a melody's notes
to combine two separate melodies into a single contrapuntal texture

example.text: The accompanist transposes the song down a third to suit the singer's range.

en.correct: the specific arrangement and spacing of the notes of a chord among the available voices or instruments
distractors: the total number of independent melodic lines active at a given moment
the process of assigning a solo passage to a particular instrument

example.text: The pianist chooses a close voicing that keeps all four chord tones within a single octave.

en.correct: the practice of having two or more voices or instruments play the same pitch or its octave simultaneously
distractors: the technique of restating a theme in twice its original note values
the process of modulating twice in quick succession

example.text: The cellos provide doubling of the bass line an octave above the double basses.

en.correct: the playing or sounding of a chord's notes in succession rather than simultaneously
distractors: the playing of two different chords at once in different keys
the gradual slowing of tempo leading into a cadence

example.text: The harpist's arpeggiation spreads each chord upward across the strings.

en.correct: the singing of multiple pitches on a single syllable of text
distractors: the singing of a single pitch across multiple syllables of text
a passage where the singer pauses entirely while the accompaniment continues

example.text: The soprano's melisma stretches the word amen across a dozen flowing notes.

en.correct: describing vocal music in which each syllable of text is set to a single note
distractors: describing vocal music in which a single syllable is stretched across many notes
describing instrumental music with no text at all

example.text: The hymn's syllabic setting makes the words easy for the congregation to follow.

en.correct: a compositional technique in which the music vividly reflects the literal meaning of the text being set
distractors: the technique of setting an entire text to a single repeated pitch
the practice of translating a text into a foreign language before setting it to music

example.text: On the word ascend, the melody uses word painting by leaping dramatically upward.

en.correct: a pedagogical system for learning counterpoint through progressively complex categories, from note-against-note to florid combinations
distractors: a style of counterpoint restricted entirely to parallel motion
a system of counterpoint used exclusively in twelve-tone composition

example.text: Students practice species counterpoint by adding a note-against-note line above a given cantus firmus.

en.correct: a flexible, expressive stretching or compressing of tempo within a phrase, without altering the overall pulse
distractors: a strict, unwavering tempo maintained throughout an entire piece
a sudden and permanent change to a new, faster tempo

example.text: The pianist's rubato lingers slightly on the melody's high point before moving on.

en.correct: an emphasis given to a note by lengthening its duration rather than by increasing its volume
distractors: an emphasis given to a note purely through increased dynamic loudness
an accent created by doubling a note at the octave

example.text: The performer creates an agogic accent by holding the downbeat slightly longer than notated.

en.correct: a technique that shifts the music's underlying pulse by reinterpreting a subdivision of the old tempo as the new beat
distractors: a technique that shifts the music into a new key using a shared pivot chord
a technique that alternates between two simultaneous meters without changing tempo

example.text: Elliott Carter's metric modulation reinterprets the eighth-note triplet as the new quarter note.

en.correct: the simultaneous use of two or more different time signatures across different parts of an ensemble
distractors: the practice of gradually accelerating tempo across a movement
a single meter that alternates its number of beats every other measure

example.text: The ensemble's polymeter has the winds playing in three-four while the strings sustain four-four.

en.correct: a larger-scale metrical organization in which groups of measures function like beats within a bigger recurring pattern
distractors: the smallest rhythmic subdivision notated within a single beat
a meter that changes its time signature every measure

example.text: The phrase's hypermeter groups four measures together as a single hypermetric unit.

en.correct: one or more unstressed notes that precede the first strong downbeat of a phrase
distractors: the final cadential note that concludes a phrase
a sustained note held beneath changing harmonies

example.text: The melody begins with a short anacrusis leading into the downbeat of the first full measure.

en.correct: a rhythmic emphasis placed on the normally weaker second and fourth beats of a measure in common time
distractors: an emphasis placed on the first beat of every measure
a rhythm created by playing three notes evenly across two beats

example.text: The drummer's snare hits mark a steady backbeat on beats two and four.

en.correct: a contrapuntal technique in which two voices trade pitches, each moving to the note previously held by the other
distractors: a technique in which one voice drops out while a new voice enters with identical material
the transposition of an entire passage between two different instruments

example.text: In the voice exchange, the soprano's note moves to the alto while the alto's note rises to the soprano.

en.correct: consecutive perfect fifths occurring between the same two voices, generally avoided in traditional voice leading
distractors: consecutive thirds occurring between the same two voices, favored in traditional voice leading
a chord progression that alternates between tonic and dominant harmonies

example.text: The exercise was marked incorrect for containing forbidden parallel fifths between the outer voices.

en.correct: a perfect fifth approached by similar motion in the outer voices, considered a weaker voice-leading fault than consecutive fifths
distractors: two perfect fifths sounding simultaneously in different octaves
a fifth interval that resolves by contrary motion into an octave

example.text: The hidden fifths between the soprano and bass are softened because the top voice moves by step.

en.correct: a major chord built on the lowered second scale degree, typically used in first inversion before the dominant
distractors: a chord built on the raised fourth scale degree used to approach the tonic
a diminished chord built entirely of stacked minor thirds

example.text: The Neapolitan sixth intensifies the harmony just before the cadence's dominant chord.

en.correct: an augmented sixth chord containing the lowered sixth scale degree, the tonic, and the raised fourth scale degree, without a fourth chord tone
distractors: an augmented sixth chord that adds both a fourth and a sixth chord tone above the bass
a chord built by stacking three consecutive perfect fourths

example.text: The Italian sixth resolves outward by half step to the dominant in both outer voices.

en.correct: an augmented sixth chord that adds the lowered third scale degree to the notes of the Italian sixth, creating a four-note sonority
distractors: an augmented sixth chord built with only three distinct pitch classes
a chord formed by stacking perfect fifths rather than thirds

example.text: The German sixth is often respelled enharmonically as a dominant seventh chord to ease the modulation.

en.correct: an augmented sixth chord that adds the second scale degree to the notes of the Italian sixth, producing a symmetrical, whole-tone-like sonority
distractors: an augmented sixth chord that adds the lowered third scale degree to the Italian sixth
a triad built from a stack of two major thirds

example.text: The French sixth's symmetrical spacing gives it a distinctly whole-tone color.

en.correct: a chord taken from the parallel major or minor key and used within a passage in the opposite mode
distractors: a chord built using only the pitches of the prevailing diatonic scale
a chord whose root is temporarily treated as a secondary tonic

example.text: The minor iv chord is a borrowed chord imported from the parallel minor key.

en.correct: a chord that functions as the dominant of a scale degree other than the tonic, temporarily tonicizing that degree
distractors: a chord built on the actual dominant scale degree of the home key
a chord that substitutes for the tonic at a deceptive cadence

example.text: The V of V is a secondary dominant that briefly tonicizes the supertonic before returning home.

en.correct: the brief treatment of a scale degree other than the tonic as if it were a temporary key center
distractors: the permanent modulation of a piece into an entirely new key
the process of raising the leading tone in a minor key

example.text: The passage's tonicization of the dominant lasts only two measures before the music returns home.

en.correct: to treat a scale degree other than the main tonic as a temporary local key center
distractors: to permanently establish a new key for the remainder of the piece
to double a melodic line at the interval of a third

example.text: The composer tonicizes the submediant briefly before the recapitulation restores the home key.

en.correct: a chord shared by two keys that is used to smoothly transition from one key to the other during a modulation
distractors: a chord used only at the very final cadence of a piece
a chord built exclusively from notes outside both the old and new key

example.text: The ii chord in the old key functions as a pivot chord, becoming the vi chord in the new key.

en.correct: a modulation that connects two otherwise unrelated keys by holding a single pitch shared between their tonic chords
distractors: a modulation achieved by using a chord that is diatonic to both keys
a modulation that respells a chord enharmonically to reach the new key

example.text: The composer sustains a single note through the common-tone modulation into the distant new key.

en.correct: a modulation achieved by reinterpreting a chord's spelling enharmonically so it functions differently in the new key
distractors: a modulation that shares a diatonic chord between the old and new keys
a modulation reached by a chain of secondary dominants

example.text: The German sixth's enharmonic modulation reinterprets it as a dominant seventh in a distant key.

en.correct: a chord whose root lies a third away from the preceding chord but that shares little diatonic relationship with it, typically involving chromatic alteration
distractors: a chord built on the diatonic third scale degree of the prevailing key
a chord that functions as the dominant of the mediant scale degree

example.text: The abrupt shift to a chromatic mediant gives the progression a striking, colorful surprise.

en.correct: the borrowing of chords or scale degrees from the parallel major or minor mode within a passage
distractors: the simultaneous combination of two entirely different modes in separate voices
the substitution of a whole-tone scale for a diatonic scale

example.text: The lowered sixth scale degree in the major-key passage results from modal mixture.

en.correct: a six-note segment of a scale or row, historically the basis of medieval solmization and later used in twelve-tone technique
distractors: a seven-note diatonic scale used in Renaissance polyphony
a chord built from six stacked perfect fifths

example.text: The composer divides the tone row into two complementary hexachords.

en.correct: an eight-note scale that alternates whole steps and half steps throughout the octave
distractors: a six-note scale built entirely from whole steps
a scale identical to the major scale but missing its seventh degree

example.text: Stravinsky's harmony frequently draws on the octatonic scale for its symmetrical color.

en.correct: a six-note scale in which every adjacent pitch is separated by a whole step, producing an ambiguous, floating quality
distractors: an eight-note scale alternating whole and half steps
a scale identical to the natural minor scale but raising the seventh degree

example.text: Debussy's whole-tone scale passage dissolves any clear sense of key.

en.correct: a seven-note scale resembling a major scale with a raised fourth and lowered seventh degree, related to the overtone series
distractors: a scale consisting only of the first five degrees of the major scale
a scale built by alternating minor thirds and half steps

example.text: The composer's use of the acoustic scale gives the passage a bright, lydian-dominant color.

en.correct: an unordered collection of pitch classes used in post-tonal analysis to describe the intervallic content of a musical passage
distractors: an ordered sequence of all twelve chromatic pitches used as a tone row
a diatonic scale containing exactly seven distinct pitches

example.text: The analyst labels the opening sonority as a particular pitch-class set to compare it with later passages.

en.correct: a category grouping intervals and their inversions together, used in post-tonal theory to measure pitch relationships regardless of octave or direction
distractors: the specific named quality and number of a single interval, such as a major third
a chord built from stacking a single recurring interval

example.text: Two intervals that are inversions of each other, like a major third and minor sixth, belong to the same interval class.

en.correct: the most compact, standardized representation of a pitch-class set used to identify and compare sets in post-tonal analysis
distractors: the original, un-transposed version of a twelve-tone row before any transformation
the initial statement of a fugue subject before any answer or countersubject

example.text: Reducing the chord to its prime form reveals that it shares the same underlying structure as an earlier sonority.

en.correct: the overall shape traced by a melody's rises and falls in pitch over time
distractors: the specific rhythmic pattern used to articulate a melody's notes
the total range in semitones between a melody's lowest and highest note

example.text: The theme's melodic contour arches upward before descending gently to its final note.

en.correct: a symmetrical four-note chord built from three stacked minor thirds, often used for its tense, ambiguous quality
distractors: a four-note chord built from three stacked major thirds
a chord formed by adding a major seventh above a major triad

example.text: The diminished seventh chord's ambiguity lets the composer resolve it to several different keys.

en.correct: a four-note chord consisting of a diminished triad with a minor seventh added above the root
distractors: a four-note chord consisting of a diminished triad with a diminished seventh added above the root
a four-note chord consisting of a major triad with a minor seventh added above the root

example.text: The half-diminished seventh chord on the leading tone often precedes the dominant in minor keys.

en.correct: a triad with an additional sixth scale degree above the root added as a color tone, common in jazz and popular harmony
distractors: a triad with an additional seventh above the root that functions as a dissonance requiring resolution
a chord built by omitting the third from a standard triad

example.text: The tune ends on a major triad with an added sixth chord for a warm, unresolved color.

en.correct: harmony built primarily from chords stacked in fourths rather than the traditional thirds
distractors: harmony built primarily from chords stacked in fifths rather than thirds
harmony that avoids any vertical stacking, relying only on melodic lines

example.text: The pianist voices the chorus using quartal harmony for an open, ambiguous sound.

en.correct: harmony built primarily from chords stacked in fifths rather than the traditional thirds
distractors: harmony built primarily from chords stacked in fourths rather than thirds
harmony consisting exclusively of major and minor triads

example.text: The composer experiments with quintal harmony, layering perfect fifths on top of one another.

en.correct: a chord formed by sounding several adjacent pitches, often a group of seconds, simultaneously
distractors: a chord formed by sounding pitches spaced a fourth apart
a rapid ornamental alternation between two adjacent notes

example.text: The pianist strikes a tone cluster with a forearm across the keys.

en.correct: the technique of moving a chord of fixed shape in parallel motion through a passage, regardless of the underlying key
distractors: the technique of resolving every dissonant chord by contrary motion
the process of gradually thinning an orchestral texture toward a single instrument

example.text: Debussy's planing slides a stack of parallel ninth chords chromatically down the keyboard.

en.correct: a system of harmony in which chords are understood in terms of their role, such as tonic, subdominant, and dominant, within a key
distractors: a system of harmony that treats all chords as equally weighted, without hierarchical roles
a system of harmony based entirely on stacked fourths rather than thirds

example.text: The analysis labels each chord according to its role within functional harmony.

en.correct: a situation in part-writing where a lower voice temporarily sounds higher in pitch than a voice normally above it
distractors: a situation where two voices sound the exact same pitch simultaneously
a situation where a voice leaps by an interval larger than an octave

example.text: The alto momentarily rises above the soprano, producing a brief voice crossing.

en.correct: the simultaneous movement of two musical lines in opposite directions
distractors: the simultaneous movement of two musical lines in the same direction by the same interval
the movement of one line while a second line remains stationary

example.text: The outer voices move in contrary motion, the soprano rising as the bass descends.

en.correct: the movement of one musical line while another remains on a single stationary pitch
distractors: the simultaneous movement of two lines in opposite directions
the movement of two lines in the same direction but by different intervals

example.text: Oblique motion occurs as the melody moves while the pedal tone in the bass holds still.

en.correct: the movement of two musical lines in the same direction, though not necessarily by the same interval
distractors: the movement of two lines in opposite directions by the same interval
the movement of one line while the other remains fixed on a single pitch

example.text: The two outer voices rise together in similar motion toward the cadence.

en.correct: a musical technique in which two or more groups of performers alternate or respond to each other, often from separated positions
distractors: a technique in which a single melody is doubled exactly at the octave
a compositional method organizing pitches through a fixed ordered row

example.text: The Venetian polychoral works exploit antiphony between choirs placed in separate galleries.

en.correct: a sustained low drone tone, often found in early music and certain folk and organ traditions
distractors: a rapid ornamental trill performed on a keyboard instrument
a short cadential formula that closes a phrase

example.text: The bagpipe's bourdon sustains beneath the melody's constantly shifting notes.

en.correct: a brief ornament consisting of a rapid alternation between a main note and an adjacent note, either above or below
distractors: a sustained ornamental trill lasting the full duration of a note
an ornamental descending scale connecting two structural notes

example.text: The keyboardist adds a quick mordent to decorate the melody's opening note.

en.correct: a continuous sliding movement from one pitch to another, passing audibly through the pitches in between
distractors: a rapid alternation between two adjacent notes performed with a single finger
a technique of plucking rather than bowing a string instrument

example.text: The harpist's glissando sweeps rapidly across the strings from low to high.

en.correct: a smooth, continuous slide between two pitches, especially characteristic of the voice or bowed strings
distractors: an abrupt, unornamented jump between two distant pitches
a technique of striking a string with the wood of the bow

example.text: The singer uses a subtle portamento to glide expressively between the two notes.

en.correct: a string-playing technique in which the wood of the bow, rather than the hair, strikes or drags across the strings
distractors: a technique in which the string is plucked rather than bowed
a technique in which the bow is played extremely close to the bridge

example.text: The eerie clattering timbre comes from the strings playing col legno.

en.correct: a string-playing technique in which the bow is drawn very close to the bridge, producing a glassy, harsh timbre
distractors: a string-playing technique in which the bow is drawn over the fingerboard for a soft, flute-like tone
a technique in which the wood of the bow strikes the strings

example.text: The violins' sul ponticello passage produces an eerie, metallic shimmer.

en.correct: a string-playing technique in which the bow is drawn over the fingerboard, producing a soft, hollow, flute-like tone
distractors: a string-playing technique in which the bow is drawn close to the bridge for a glassy tone
a technique in which the strings are struck with the wood of the bow

example.text: The cellos switch to sul tasto for the hushed opening of the movement.

en.correct: an instruction in orchestral writing indicating that a section should split into separate parts to play different notes simultaneously
distractors: an instruction indicating that an entire section should play in unison on a single pitch
an instruction indicating that a section should stop playing entirely

example.text: The violas split into divisi to sustain a four-note chord.

en.correct: a direction in a musical part indicating that the performer is silent for an extended passage or movement
distractors: a direction indicating that a passage should be played as loudly as possible
a direction indicating that a performer should improvise freely

example.text: The trumpet part is marked tacet for the entire second movement.

en.correct: an extended technique on a wind or string instrument that produces more than one pitch simultaneously from a single instrument
distractors: a technique in which several instruments double the same single pitch
a technique of rapidly alternating between two written pitches

example.text: The saxophonist produces eerie multiphonics by altering the embouchure and fingering simultaneously.

en.correct: a piano whose sound is altered by placing objects such as screws, bolts, or rubber between or on its strings
distractors: a piano tuned to a nonstandard microtonal system before performance
a piano equipped with an extended keyboard range beyond the standard octaves

example.text: John Cage's prepared piano transforms the instrument's familiar timbre into something percussive and metallic.

en.correct: a compositional technique in which a single melodic line is distributed across changing instrumental timbres rather than kept in one instrument
distractors: a technique in which a melody is repeated at increasingly faster tempos
a technique in which the same pitch is sustained across an entire movement

example.text: Webern's orchestration exemplifies Klangfarbenmelodie, passing single notes of a melody between different instruments.

en.correct: a vocal technique halfway between speech and song, in which pitches are approximated rather than sustained precisely
distractors: a vocal technique requiring exact, sustained pitch with no rhythmic flexibility
a vocal technique in which multiple singers speak the same text simultaneously

example.text: Schoenberg's Pierrot Lunaire calls for Sprechstimme, notating approximate pitches for a speech-like delivery.

en.correct: in Schenkerian analysis, the fundamental descending melodic line believed to underlie a tonal composition's structure
distractors: in Schenkerian analysis, the surface-level ornamented melody as literally notated in the score
a term for the opening theme of a sonata-form exposition

example.text: The analyst reduces the melody to its Urlinie, a simple stepwise descent to the tonic.

en.correct: in Schenkerian analysis, the fundamental structure combining the basic melodic descent and bass arpeggiation that underlies a tonal work
distractors: in Schenkerian analysis, the fully ornamented foreground version of a piece as performed
a term describing the closing cadence of a Baroque suite

example.text: Schenker argued that nearly all tonal masterworks can be reduced to a single underlying Ursatz.

en.correct: an analytical method that reduces a tonal composition to hierarchical layers, revealing an underlying fundamental structure
distractors: an analytical method that classifies chords solely by their surface-level roman numerals
an analytical method used exclusively to study twelve-tone rows

example.text: Schenkerian analysis reveals how the piece's elaborate surface decorates a simple underlying melodic descent.

en.correct: chromatic alterations applied by performers to notes in early music that were not always explicitly notated in the original source
distractors: a genre of purely instrumental Renaissance dance music
a term for improvised ornamentation added only in the final cadence

example.text: Editors mark suggested musica ficta above the staff to indicate accidentals the singers likely added.

en.correct: an early medieval form of polyphony in which one or more voices are added to a plainchant melody
distractors: a solo unaccompanied chant sung without any added voices
a Renaissance instrumental dance form in triple meter

example.text: Early organum simply doubled the chant a fourth or fifth below the original melody.

en.correct: a medieval compositional technique in which a melody is broken up between two or more voices, each resting while the other sounds
distractors: a technique in which two voices sing the identical melody simultaneously in unison
a technique of sustaining a single drone beneath a moving melody

example.text: The motet's hocket rapidly tosses fragments of the melody back and forth between voices.

en.correct: a short bass line repeated continuously throughout a piece while the upper voices vary above it
distractors: a bass line that is played only once at the very opening of a piece
a technique in which the bass line inverts the melody of the upper voice

example.text: Purcell's aria unfolds over a haunting, repeating ground bass in the lowest voice.

en.correct: a Baroque compositional form built from continuous variations over a short repeating harmonic or bass pattern, typically in triple meter
distractors: a fast, contrapuntal form built from successive imitative entries of a single subject
a strophic vocal form in which the same music repeats unchanged for every verse

example.text: Bach's chaconne for solo violin spins dozens of variations from a single repeating harmonic pattern.
